title: When news becomes distressing: Crisis-related media consumption and empathic distress
summary: News about wars, natural disasters, or pandemics can be emotionally overwhelming. People who frequently consume such content may experience feelings of helplessness and emotional distress in response to the suffering of others. This study examines whether and how strongly crisis-related news consumption is linked to this kind of empathic distress. It also explores which personal characteristics – such as emotion regulation skills, mindfulness, or personality traits – may strengthen or weaken this relationship. Data are collected once via an online questionnaire taking approximately 45 minutes.
conditions: This study investigates empathic distress as a psychological health outcome associated with crisis-related media consumption. Empathic distress refers to a self-oriented aversive emotional state triggered by exposure to others' suffering — characterized by feelings of overwhelm, helplessness, and emotional burden. Repeated exposure to crisis-related news content (e.g., wars, natural disasters, pandemics) may overload empathy and stress systems, potentially contributing to emotional withdrawal and reduced empathic responsiveness. The study examines individual protective and risk factors — including emotion regulation, dispositional mindfulness, neuroticism, age, and gender — that moderate the relationship between news consumption and empathic distress.
